Chapter 7. The Literary World—Friendships, Rivalries, and the Search for Belonging.
The world of writers... it's a curious place, isn't it? On one hand, it feels incredibly close-knit and supportive—like you’re finally among people who just get it. But at the same time, there’s this underlying tension, a sense of competition that you can’t quite shake.
If you’ve ever felt like an outsider, stepping into this world is both thrilling and a little overwhelming. You meet people who become true friends—maybe over late-night talks, swapping stories about rejection letters, or celebrating small wins together. But, let’s be honest, there are also rivalries simmering in the background. Sometimes, you can almost feel it in the room.
At those literary gatherings, ambition and insecurity hang in the air. You’ll hear some writers casually bragging about their latest success, while others try to hide that little sting of disappointment. There’s this constant urge to measure yourself against everyone else—to wonder, "Am I good enough? Am I doing enough?" It can push you forward, but if you’re not careful, it might eat away at why you started writing in the first place.
But here’s the beautiful part: even in all that noise, real friendships can take root. Imagine two writers, both a little unsure, finding common ground simply because they love words, or they respect each other’s work. Those connections can become a lifeline, a reminder that, even in a world filled with competition, you’re not actually alone.
And then there are the mentors. The older writers who pull you aside, share a bit of wisdom, or just listen when you need it most. Sometimes their advice is tough to hear, but it’s usually exactly what you need. Think about all the wisdom that gets passed down quietly—maybe over a cup of tea, or during a long walk through the city. Most people never see those moments, but they make all the difference.
Of course, the literary world isn’t always kind. Sometimes you’ll face broken promises, missed opportunities, or get caught up in the politics of publishing. That can really sting. But there are also moments of unexpected grace—a kind word from someone you admire, a surprise award, or that magical day when your book finally finds its readers.
Over time, you learn how to move through this world with a bit more humility, and just enough confidence. The search for belonging? It never fully goes away, but it becomes less pressing. What really matters, in the end, is the work itself—and the relationships that lift you up along the way.
